An excellent example of prudence and piety.</ns0:note>, and took bread <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">By which may be here understood all necessaries, as <ns0:hi>Mal.</ns0:hi> 1. 7, 12. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6. 11. and 14. 15. com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pared with <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 6. 36. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 14. 1.</ns0:note>, and a bottle of water, and gave <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> unto Hagar (putting <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> on her shoulder) and the child, and sent her away <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> How is it like<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly that so rich and liberal a person as <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> would send away such near and dear Relations with so mean accommo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dations? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> 1. This might be done by particular command from God to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> though it be not here expressed, as ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny things were said by God and done by men, which are not mentioned in Scripture, as is evident from <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 20. 30, 31. and 21. 25. and many other places. And God might order it thus, partly to chastise <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> irregular Marriage with <ns0:hi>Hagar;</ns0:hi> partly to correct and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ame the haughty and rugged temper of the Bond-woman and her Son; and to prepare them for the receiving of Gods help and mercy; and partly that he might more eminently shew his care and kindness to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> in providing for such forlorn and neglected Creatures, because they belonged to him. 2. It cannot be reasonably doubted, that <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> gave her these Provisions onely for the present, and intended to send further and better afterward to a place appointed by him, which also he did. But she mis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed her way, as well might, in the Wilderness, and thereby came into these straits designed by God for the signification of greater Mysteries, as may be gathered from <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.</ns0:note>: and she de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parted, and wandred in the wilderness of Beer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sheba <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">A place near <ns0:hi>Gerar,</ns0:hi> so called here by a Prolepsis. See <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 31.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And the water was spent in the bottle, and she cast the child <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Not as if she carried him in her arms or upon her shoul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ders, for he was now about eighteen year old, but being weak and faint and no doubt much dejected in spirit upon the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spect of his desolate and distressed condition, she was forced to support and lead him by the hand, but now, despairing of his life, she lays him down under a shrub.</ns0:note> under one of the shrubs.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And she went, and sat her down over against <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> a good way off, as it were a bow-shot: for she said, let me not see the death of the child. And she sat over against <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> and lift up her voice and wept <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Who wept? Either <ns0:hi>Hagar,</ns0:hi> for the verb is of the femi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nine gender; or the Lad, as the words following seem to intimate. And for the change of Genders, that is not infrequent in Scripture use.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And God heard the voice of the lad <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He heard his cries tho' not flowing from true Repentance, but extorted from him by his pressing calamity.</ns0:note>, and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, what aileth thee, Hagar? fear not: for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Though he be in a vast and desolate Wilderness, yet my eye is upon him, and I will take care of him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 Arise, lift up the lad, and hold him in thine hand: for I will make him a great nation.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>b (i. e.</ns0:hi>) Support or sustain thy languishing child with thy hand; for I will bless him and thy care shall not be in vain.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And God opened her eyes <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not that her eyes were shut or blind before, but she saw not the Well before; either because it was at some distance, or because her eyes were full of tears, and her mind distracted and heedless through excessive grief and fear; or because God with-held her eyes that she might not see it without his infor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mation. Compare <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 22, 31. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 24. 16.</ns0:note>, and she saw a well of water, and she went, and filled the bottle with water, and gave the lad drink.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And God was with the lad, and he grew, and dwelt in the wilderness, and became an Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cher <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) A skilful Hunter of Beasts and Warriour with men too, according to the prediction, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 16. 12. For the bow was a principal instrument in War as well as in Hunting, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 48. 22. & 49. 23, 24. And these two professions oft went together. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 10. 9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:23" />21 And he dwelt in th wilderness of Paran <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">In the borders of that Wilderness, by comparing <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 14. 6. for the innermost parts of it were uninhabitable by Men or Beasts, as antient Writers note.</ns0:note>: and his mother took him a wife <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">By which we see both the obligation that lies upon Parents, and the right that is invested in them, to dispose of their Children in Marriage in convenient time. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 24. 4. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 28. 2. <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 14. 2.</ns0:note> out of the land of Egypt <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther than out of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> concerning whose accursed state and future destruction she had been informed in <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> house.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And it came to pass at that time, that Abi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />melech <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">He of whom see <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 20. 2.</ns0:note>, and Phicol, the chief captain of his host, spake unto Abraham, saying, God <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> with thee in all that thou doest <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">We plainly see that God blesseth and prospereth thee in all thy undertakings.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 Now therefore swear unto me here by God, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> if thou shalt lie unto me.</ns0:note> that thou wilt not deal falsly with me <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">That thou wilt not do me any hurt or injury: Heb. <ns0:hi>that thou wilt not lie unto me, i. e.</ns0:hi> As thou hast formerly professed kindness and friendship to me, give me thy Oath to assure me that thou wilt be true and constant to thy own professions.</ns0:note>, nor with my son, nor with my sons son, <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to the kindness that I have done unto thee, thou shalt do unto me, and to the land wherein thou hast sojourned.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And Abraham said, I will swear <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> How could <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> lawfully swear this, when <ns0:hi>Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />naan</ns0:hi> was given by God to him and his seed for ever? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> Neither <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> nor his seed had any present and actual right to the possession of the Land, but onely the promise of a right in it, and possession of it after some hundreds of years, and therefore he gave away none of his right by this Oath. For this Oath did only oblige <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> and not his Posterity, and <ns0:hi>Abi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />melech</ns0:hi> extended that obligation no further than to his Sons Son.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And Abraham reproved Abimelech <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">That the foundation of true Friendship might be firmly laid, and the peace inviolably observed, he removes an im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pediment to it, an occasion of quarrel and just exception on <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> part.</ns0:note>, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause of a well of water <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Which in those hot and dry Countries was of great esteem and necessity. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen,</ns0:hi> 26. 19, 20, 21. <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 1. 15. Besides <ns0:hi>a Well</ns0:hi> may be put for <ns0:hi>Wells,</ns0:hi> as the Greeks render it, and as may seem probable by comparing this with <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 26. 15, 18. It being an ordinary thing to use the singu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lar number for the plural, as hath been shewed. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 3. 2. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 4. 20.</ns0:note> which Abimelechs ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants had violently taken away.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And Abimelech said, I wot not who hath done this thing: neither didst thou tell me, nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther yet heard I <ns0:hi>of it,</ns0:hi> but to day <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">By which he wisely and truly suggests, that <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> should not have smothered the grudge in his mind so long time, but should instantly have reproved him for it, and endeavoured a speedy redress, which hereby he intimates that he was ready to give.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And Abraham took sheep and oxen, and gave them unto Abimelech <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Partly as an acknowledgment to him for his former favour and Friendship; partly as an assurance of his sincere Friendship both present and for the future, of his aquiescence in his answer about the Well; and partly for Sacrifice, and for the usual Rite in making Covenants, which was that the persons Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venanting might pass through the parts of the slain Beasts. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 15. 18.</ns0:note>: and both of them made a covenant.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And Abraham set seven ew-lambs of the flock by themselves.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 And Abimelech said unto Abraham, what <ns0:hi>mean</ns0:hi> these seven ew-lambs, which thou hast set by themselves?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And he said, For <ns0:hi>these</ns0:hi> seven ew-lambs, shalt thou take of my hand, that they may be a witness unto me, that I have digged this well <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That this care of <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> was not superfluous may ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pear from <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 26. 15.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 Wherefore he called that place <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">That is, <ns0:hi>the well of the Oath.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Beer-she<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ba <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Which name was communicated unto a City adjoyning: Of which see <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 26. 23. <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 15. 28. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 17. 11. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 24. 2.</ns0:note>, because there they sware both of them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 Thus they made a covenant at Beer-sheba: then Abimelech rose up, and Phicol the chief cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain of his host, and they returned into the land of the Philistines <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> Into their part of that Land, to wit <ns0:hi>Gerar,</ns0:hi> which was not far from this place. It is an usual synecdoche, whereby the whole Land is put for a part of it: Otherwise they were at this time in that Land.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> planted a <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> T<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e.</ns0:note> Grove <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Not so much for shade, which yet was pleasant and ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary in these hot Regions, as for religious use, that he might retire thither from the noise of worldly business, and freely converse with his maker. Which practice of his was afterwards abused to superstition and Idolatry, for which reason Groves were commanded to be cut down. See <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 12. 2. and 16. 21.</ns0:note> in Beer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sheba, and called there on the Name of the LORD <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Thankfully acknowledging Gods great goodness in giv<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing him the favour and friendship of so great and worthy a Prince and Neighbour.</ns0:note>, the everlasting God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34 And Abraham sojourned in the Philistins land many days.</ns0:p>
